questions.q: The plot that depicts the behavior of the mean free time $τ$ (time between two successive collisions) for the molecules of an ideal gas, as a function of temperature $\left(T\right),$ qualitatively, is: (Graphs are schematic and not drawn to scale)
questions.solution:
The average time taken by a moving particle between successive collisions or impacts is referred to as the mean free time $\left(τ\right)$.

The average distance a moving particle travels between successive collisions or impacts is referred to as the mean free path $\left(\lambda\right)$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{kT}{\sqrt{2}\pi{d}^{2}P}$

and ${v}_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$

So, the mean free time $τ = \dfrac{\lambda}{{v}_{rms}}$

Therefore, $τ ∝ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$

questions.q: Consider a gas of triatomic molecules. The molecules are assumed to be triangular and made of massless rigid rods whose vertices are occupied by atoms. The internal energy of a mole of the gas at temperature T is:
questions.solution:
The formula of internal energy of a gas is given by

$U = \dfrac{f}{2}RT$

Here $R$ is the gas constant and $T$ is temperature.

$\left(R = 8 . 314J{mol}^{- 1}{K}^{- 1}\right)$

For the given configuration of triatomic molecules, the degree of freedom $f = 6$

$⇒ U = \dfrac{6}{2}RT = 3RT$

questions.q: A gas has $n$ degrees of freedom. The ratio of specific heat of gas at constant volume to the specific heat of gas at constant pressure will be
questions.solution:
For a gas having degrees of freedom $n$,

${C}_{V} = \dfrac{nR}{2}$ and using Mayer's relation ${C}_{P} = {C}_{V} + R$. Therefore,

$\dfrac{{C}_{V}}{{C}_{P}} = \dfrac{n}{n + 2}$.

questions.q:
Same gas is filled in two vessels of the same volume at the same temperature. If the ratio of the number of molecules is $1: 4$, then

$A$. The r.m.s. velocity of gas molecules in two vessels will be the same.

$B$. The ratio of pressure in these vessels will be $1: 4$.

$C$. The ratio of pressure will be $1: 1$.

$D$. The r.m.s. velocity of gas molecules in two vessels will be in the ratio of $1: 4$.
questions.solution:
The rms velocity of a gas is given by ${V}_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$. Therefore,${V}_{rms}$ is independent of number of moles, Hence, statement A is correct and D is incorrect.

According to the ideal gas equation $PV = nRT ⇒ P ∝ n$

$⇒ \dfrac{{P}_{1}}{{P}_{2}} = \dfrac{{n}_{1}}{{n}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Hence, statement B is correct and C is incorrect.

Ans [$A \text{ and } B$ only are correct]

questions.q:
Which statements are correct about degrees of freedom?

A. A molecule with $n$ degrees of freedom has ${n}^{2}$ different ways of storing energy.

B. Each degree of freedom is associated with $\dfrac{1}{2}RT$ average energy per mole.

C. A monoatomic gas molecule has $1$ rotational degree of freedom where as diatomic molecule has $2$ rotational degrees of freedom

D. ${CH}_{4}$ has a total to $6$ degrees of freedom.

Choose the correct answer from the option given below:
questions.solution:
According to the equipartition of energy, each degree of freedom carries $\dfrac{1}{2}RT$ energy per mole and total energy per mole of a gas having $n$ degrees of freedom is $\dfrac{1}{2}nRT$. Therefore, statement A is wrong and statement B is correct.

A monoatomic molecule only has translational degrees of freedom and does not have rotational degree of freedom. For a polyatomic model there are three rotational degrees of freedom and three translational degrees of freedom. Therefore, statement C is incorrect and statement D is correct.

questions.q:
A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen has volume $2000{cm}^{3}$, temperature $300K$, pressure $100kPa$ and mass $0 . 76g$. The ratio of number of moles of hydrogen to number of moles of oxygen in the mixture will be

[Take gas constant $R = 8 . 3J{K}^{- 1}{mol}^{- 1}$]
questions.solution:
From the ideal gas equation, total number of moles in the mixture are,

$n = \dfrac{PV}{RT} = \dfrac{2 \times {10}^{- 3} \times 100 \times {10}^{3} \times 3}{25 \times 300}$$⇒ n = \dfrac{2}{25} = 0 . 08$

If number of moles of oxygen are ${n}_{1}$ and of hydrogen are ${n}_{2}$

${n}_{1} + {n}_{2} = n = 0 . 08 \ldots \left(1\right)$

And total mass of the mixture

${n}_{1}\left(32\right) + {n}_{2}\left(2\right) = 0 . 76 \ldots \left(2\right)$

Solving the above equations,

${n}_{1} = 0 . 02$ and ${n}_{2} = 0 . 06$

$\dfrac{{n}_{2}}{{n}_{1}} = 3$

questions.q: The number of air molecules per ${cm}^{3}$ is increased from $3 \times {10}^{19}$ to $12 \times {10}^{19} .$ The ratio of collision frequency of air molecules before and after the increase in number respectively is :
questions.solution:
The given data is

${n}_{1} = 3 \times {10}^{19}{n}_{2} = 12 \times {10}^{19}$

The mean time between two collision has the meaning of a period $τ$, since it indicates the repetitive time intervals in which on average collisions take place. The reciprocal of the time $τ$ can be understood as the collision frequency$f$, which indicates the number of collisions per unit time.The collision frequency is also directly proportional to the number molecules per unit volume.

$f ∝ \dfrac{1}{τ}$

$⇒ f ∝ n$

$⇒ \dfrac{{f}_{\text{1}}}{{f}_{\text{2}}} = \dfrac{{n}_{1}}{{n}_{2}} = \dfrac{3 \times {10}^{19}}{12 \times {10}^{19}} = 0 . 25$

The mean free path is given by the relation,

Hence,

$\dfrac{1500d}{\lambda '} = \dfrac{273}{373}$

$⇒ {\lambda}^{'} = 2049 . 45d \approx 2049d$

questions.q:
The $rms$ speed of oxygen molecule in a vessel at particular temperature is $\left(1 + \dfrac{5}{x}\right)\dfrac{1}{2}v,$ when $v$ is the average speed of the molecule. The value of $x$ will be:

(take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution:
The RMS speed is given by

${v}_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$

The average speed is given by

${v}_{avg} = \sqrt{\dfrac{8RT}{\piM}}$

The ratio is

$⇒ \dfrac{{v}_{rms}}{{v}_{\text{avg}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}{\dfrac{8RT}{\piM}} =}\sqrt{\dfrac{3\pi}{8}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{8} \times \dfrac{22}{7}} ⇒ \dfrac{{v}_{rms}}{{v}_{\text{avg}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{33}{28}}$

Comparing it with the given value $\left(1 + \dfrac{5}{x}\right)\dfrac{1}{2}$,

$\dfrac{{v}_{rms}}{{v}_{\text{avg}}} = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{5}{28}} ⇒ x = 28$

questions.q: Two thin metallic spherical shells of radii ${r}_{1}$ and ${r}_{2}\left({r}_{1} < {r}_{2}\right)$ are placed with their centres coinciding. A material of thermal conductivity $K$ is filled in the space between the shells. The inner shell is maintained at temperature ${\theta}_{1}$ and the outer shell at temperature ${\theta}_{2}\left({\theta}_{1} < {\theta}_{2}\right) .$ The rate at which heat flows radially through the material is :
questions.solution:
Equivalent resistance $( R ) = \dfrac{{r}_{2} - {r}_{1}}{K4\pi{r}_{2}{r}_{1}}$
Thus, Heat flow $= \dfrac{4\piK\left({r}_{1}{r}_{2}\right)\left({\theta}_{2} - {\theta}_{1}\right)}{\left({r}_{2} - {r}_{1}\right)}$

questions.q: A cylinder of fixed capacity of $44 . 8$ litres contains helium gas at standard temperature and pressure. The amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of gas in the cylinder by $20 . 0 ° C$ will be (Given gas constant $R = 8 . 3J{K}^{- 1}{mol}^{- 1}$)
questions.solution:
At STP volume occupied by one mole of a gas is $22 . 4L$. Therefore, number of moles are, $n = \dfrac{44 . 8}{22 . 4} = 2mol$.

The process is isochoric process as the volume of the cylinder remains fixed and helium is a monatomic gas. Therefore, amount of heat needed will be,

$Q = n Cv \DeltaT = \left(2\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{2}R\right)\left(20\right) = 3 \times 8 . 3 \times 20 = 498J$

questions.q:
At what temperature a gold ring of diameter $6 . 230cm$ be heated so that it can be fitted on a wooden bangle of diameter $6 . 241cm$? Both the diameters have been measured at room temperature $\left(27 ° C\right)$.
(Given: coefficient of linear thermal expansion of gold ${\alpha}_{L} = 1 . 4 \times {10}^{- 5}{K}^{- 1}$)
questions.solution:
To fit gold ring of diameter $5 . 230cm$ over wooden bangle of diameter $6 . 241cm$, gold ring expansion is required.

So, $l = {l}_{0}\left[1 + \alpha\DeltaT\right]$

$⇒ 6 . 241 = 6 . 230\left[1 + 1 . 4 \times {10}^{- 5}\left(T - 27\right)\right]$

$⇒ \dfrac{6 . 241}{6 . 230} - 1 = 1 . 4 \times {10}^{- 5}\left(T - 27\right)$

$⇒ T = 152 . 7 ° C$

questions.q: $1kg$ of water at $100 ° C$ is converted into steam at $100 ° C$ by boiling at atmospheric pressure. The volume of water changes from $1 . 00 \times {10}^{- 3}{m}^{3}$ as a liquid to $1 . 671{m}^{3}$ as steam. The change in internal energy of the system during the process will be (Given latent heat of vaporisation $= 2257kJ / kg$, Atmospheric pressure $\left= 1 \times {10}^{5}Pa\right)$
questions.solution:
The work to be done in the process is given by

$\begin{cases}dW & = & PdV \\ = & 1 \times {10}^{5}Pa \times ( 1 . 671 - 0 . 001 ) {m}^{3} \\ = & 1 . 670 \times {10}^{5}J\end{cases}$

The change in heat energy during the vaporisation process can be calculated as follows-

$\begin{cases}\Delta{Q}_{\text{supplied}} & = & 2257 \times 1 \times {10}^{3}J \\ = & 22 . 57 \times {10}^{5}J\end{cases}$

Hence, the change in internal energy in the process is given by

$\begin{cases}\DeltaU & = & \Delta{Q}_{supplied} - \DeltaW \\ = & ( 22 . 57 - 1 . 67 ) \times {10}^{5}J \\ = & 20 . 9 \times {10}^{5}J \\ = & 2090kJ\end{cases}$

questions.q: If one mole of an ideal gas at $\left({P}_{1}, {V}_{1}\right)$ is allowed to expand reversibly and isothermally ($A$ to $B$) its pressure is reduced to one-half of the original pressure (see figure). This is followed by a constant volume cooling till its pressure is reduced to one-fourth of the initial value $\left(B \to C\right) .$ Then it is restored to its initial state by a reversible adiabatic compression ($C$ to $A$). The net workdone by the gas is equal to:
questions.solution:
$A - B =$ isothermal process

${W}_{AB} = {P}_{1}{V}_{1}ln\left[\dfrac{2{V}_{1}}{{V}_{1}}\right] = {P}_{1}{V}_{1}ln\left(2\right)$

$B - C \to$ Isochoric process

${W}_{BC} = 0$

$C - A \to$Adiabatic process

${W}_{CA} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} - \dfrac{{P}_{1}}{4} \times 2{V}_{1}}{1 - \gamma} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}\left[1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right]}{1 - \gamma} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{2\left(1 - \gamma\right)}$

${W}_{net} = {W}_{AB} + {W}_{BC} + {W}_{CA}\left\{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} = RT\right\}$

$= {P}_{1}{V}_{1}ln\left(2\right) + 0 + \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{2\left(1 - \gamma\right)}$

${W}_{net} = RT\left[ln\left(2\right) - \dfrac{1}{2\left(\gamma - 1\right)}\right]$

questions.q: One mole of an ideal gas is taken through an adiabatic process where the temperature rises from $27 ° C$ to $37 ° C$. If the ideal gas is composed of polyatomic molecule that has 4 vibrational modes, which of the following is true? $\left[R = 8 . 314J{mol}^{- 1}{k}^{- 1}\right]$
options: work done by the gas is close to $332J$
work done on the gas is close to $582J$
work done by the gas is close to $582J$
work done on the gas is close to $332J$
questions.solution:
Since, each vibrational mode, corresponds to two degrees of freedom, hence, $f =3 ( trans .) +3( rot . )+8( vib . )=14$

$\text{ and } \gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{f}$

$\gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{14} = \dfrac{8}{7}$

$W = \dfrac{nR\DeltaT}{\gamma - 1} = - 582$

As $W < 0$. work is done on the gas.

questions.q: A certain amount of gas of volume $V$ at $27 ° C$ temperature and pressure $2 \times {10}^{7}N{m}^{- 2}$ expands isothermally until its volume gets doubled. Later it expands adiabatically until its volume gets redoubled. The final pressure of the gas will be (Use $\gamma = 1 . 5$)
questions.solution:
Given here, ${P}_{1} = 2 \times {10}^{7}N{m}^{- 2} = 2 \times {10}^{7}Pa$

Using Boyle's law,

${P}_{1}{V}_{1} = {P}_{2}{V}_{2}$

Since ${V}_{2} = 2{V}_{1}$.

Hence, ${P}_{2} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}}{2}$ (isothermal expansion)

${P}_{2} = 1 \times {10}^{7}Pa$

Now, during adiabatic expansion,

${P}_{2}{\left({V}_{2}\right)}^{\gamma} = {P}_{3}{\left(2{V}_{2}\right)}^{\gamma}$

${P}_{3} = \dfrac{1 \times {10}^{7}}{{2}^{1 . 5}} = 3 . 536 \times {10}^{6}Pa$

questions.q: In an Isothermal change, the change in pressure and volume of a gas can be represented for three different temperature; ${T}_{3} > {T}_{2} > {T}_{1}$ as:
questions.solution:
In case of isothermal process, pressure vs volume graph is a rectangular hyperbola.

The graph of the isothermal process shifts away from the origin as the temperature of the process is increased. Thus, the curve away from the origin ${T}_{3}$ have the highest temperature whereas the curve closer to the origin ${T}_{1}$ have the lowest temperature.

Here, the dotted line shows the isobaric line that implies ${T}_{3} > {T}_{2} > {T}_{1}$ as $T = \dfrac{PV}{nR}$.

questions.q: Let ${\gamma}_{1}$ be the ratio of molar specific heat at constant pressure and molar specific heat at constant volume of a monoatomic gas and ${\gamma}_{2}$ be the similar ratio of diatomic gas. Considering the diatomic gas molecule as a rigid rotator, the ratio $\dfrac{{\gamma}_{1}}{{\gamma}_{2}}$ is:
questions.solution:
As we know, ${C}_{v} = f\dfrac{R}{2}$

and ${C}_{p} = {C}_{v} + R = f\dfrac{R}{2} + R$

Therefore, $\gamma = \dfrac{{C}_{p}}{{C}_{v}} = 1 + \dfrac{2}{f}$

For monatomic gas, $f = 3$ and hence ${\gamma}_{1} = \dfrac{5}{3}$

For diatomic gas, $f = 5$ and hence ${\gamma}_{2} = \dfrac{7}{5}$

Required ratio, $\dfrac{{\gamma}_{1}}{{\gamma}_{2}} = \dfrac{25}{21}$

questions.q: A hypothetical gas expands adiabatically such that its volume changes from $08$ litres to $27$ litres. If the ratio of final pressure of the gas to initial pressure of the gas is$\dfrac{16}{81}$ . Then the ratio of $\dfrac{{C}_{p}}{{C}_{v}}$ will be.
questions.solution:
Let $\gamma$ be the ratio of $\dfrac{{C}_{p}}{{C}_{v}}$.

Then for adiabatic process $P{V}^{\gamma} =$Constant

$⇒ \dfrac{{P}_{i}}{{P}_{f}} = {\left(\dfrac{{V}_{f}}{{V}_{i}}\right)}^{\gamma}$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{81}{16}\right) = {\left(\dfrac{27}{8}\right)}^{\gamma} ⇒ \left[{\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)}^{3}\right]\dfrac{4}{3} = {\left(\dfrac{27}{8}\right)}^{\gamma}$

$⇒ \gamma = \dfrac{4}{3}$
